body:
An anomaly detector that flags something new has not told you what it is.

That gap is wider than most of us assume. In one published open-vocabulary video study, novel categories were detected at 88.2 AUC on UCF-Crime. The same model named them correctly 37.1 percent of the time, even with every right name in the vocabulary. Those are that study's numbers, not mine.

In my paper I argue that "explanation" in anomaly detection hides three separate claims:

→ A score claim: which parts of the input raised the score. The detector can check it.
→ A deviation claim: in what respect the input differs from the reference data. The reference data can check it.
→ A name claim: what the thing actually is. Only a label, a benchmark description or a person can check it.

I assembled published results rather than running new experiments. One finding stuck with me: a detector can flag an image correctly while the names it generated for it are wrong. And I found no study that measures, on the same instances, whether the name is right and whether it names what the detector responded to.

If your system shows users a name next to an alert, validate that name against ground truth. Do not borrow trust from the detection score.

The full paper is attached below.
question: When your detector flags something, who or what tells you what it actually is?
